---
title: "Beyond the clock score"
subtitle: "Reading an aging methylome without predicting an age"
toc: true
toc-depth: 3
---

Every clock in the catalogue models the *mean* beta at a set of sites and returns one number.
That is not the only thing a methylation matrix can be asked, and on the field's own evidence it
may not be the most informative thing.

Tong et al. [[65]](references.qmd#ref-65) quantified how much of a clock is entropy rather than
biology: roughly 66 to 75 per cent of Horvath2013's accuracy against chronological age is
reproducible by a purely stochastic model of methylation change, about 90 per cent for Zhang, and
about 63 per cent for PhenoAge. The gradient is the interesting part. The more accurately a clock
predicts chronological age, the more of it is drift.

This page covers the three things FALCONAge computes that are not clocks: the disorder readouts,
repertoire structure, and where a clock's coefficient mass sits. None of them returns an age, none
is gated by `scale_type`, and none is comparable between datasets processed differently.

## Disorder: entropy, drift and the barometer

`falconage.disorder` holds four functions, and the division between them is about *what carries
the number*, which is the distinction most easily lost.

| Function | Returns | Per what |
|---|---|---|
| `fa.entropy` | how far the methylome sits from fully committed | sample |
| `fa.drift` | how far a sample sits from the cohort centroid | sample |
| `fa.noise_barometer` | summed per-site SD over age-variable sites | **group** |
| `fa.variable_sites` | which cytosines widen with age | site |

### Entropy

Normalised Shannon entropy over the beta matrix:

$$
S = \frac{1}{N \log \tfrac{1}{2}} \sum_{i=1}^{N}
    \Big[ \beta_i \log \beta_i + (1-\beta_i) \log (1-\beta_i) \Big]
$$

Bounded 0 to 1. A site at beta 0 or 1 is decided and contributes nothing; a site at 0.5 is
maximally uncertain and contributes its full share. So $S = 0$ is a methylome where every site is
committed and $S = 1$ is one where none of them is.

```python
import falconage as fa

data = fa.read("betas.csv")
ent = fa.entropy(data)        # entropy, n_sites
```

`n_sites` is not decoration. Entropy is a *mean over sites*, so a mean over different sites is not
a comparison. The default restricts to sites covered in every sample for exactly that reason; set
`complete_sites=False` to use each sample's own coverage and then read `n_sites` before comparing
any two rows.

On the test corpus this lands at 0.695 with an SD of 0.007 across 825,177 complete sites, which is
what a clean bimodal EPIC distribution looks like once it is summarised to one number.

### Drift

The barometer is a property of a group, which leaves nothing to regress against an outcome.
`fa.drift` is the per-sample analogue: the distance from the cohort centroid, computed
**leave-one-out** so that a sample is never scored against a mean it helped compute.

```python
dri = fa.drift(data)                          # drift from this cohort
dri = fa.drift(data, reference=young_mean)    # drift from a young reference
```

The leave-one-out default matters more than it looks. Scoring a sample against a centroid that
includes it shrinks its own distance, and in a small cohort that shrinkage is large enough to
invert a group difference.

### Which sites actually widen

The barometer of Mei et al. [[70]](references.qmd#ref-70) is defined over "cytosines whose variance
rises with age", and that clause is the whole statistic. Summed over every site instead, the sum
is dominated by sites that are merely variable, most of which have nothing to do with age.

`fa.variable_sites` is that selection step, split out so it can be inspected rather than assumed.
The test is Brown-Forsythe, which is Levene's test using the median, across age bins. Bartlett's
test is the more common choice in this literature and is the wrong one here: it assumes normality
within each group, and beta values near 0 or 1 are visibly not normal, so Bartlett reports
variance differences that are distributional artefacts.

A significant result says the variances *differ* between bins. It does not say variance *rises*,
and a site whose variance falls is just as significant, so `direction` carries the sign of the
trend and `rising` is the conjunction the barometer wants.

::: {.callout-important}
## What this looks like on a cohort that is too small

Run on the test corpus, `sites_rising` under Benjamini-Hochberg is **zero**. Twenty-seven samples
in three bins of nine, against roughly 820,000 tests, has almost no power once the correction is
applied.

That is the correct answer, not a gap in the implementation. A barometer that means anything needs
a cohort in the hundreds. `fa.noise_barometer` accepts an explicit `sites=` list so a selection
made elsewhere can be reused, which is also the only way the statistic transfers between cohorts.
:::

## Repertoire structure

`falconage.immune` addresses a covariate no published blood clock carries.

Deconvolution answers *how many cells of each type*. It says nothing about *how many distinct
clones those cells represent*, and the two are different measurements: two donors with an
identical CD8 memory fraction can differ by orders of magnitude in clone count.

### Why clone count should move a clock at all

Take one cell type holding fraction $f$ of the sample, split into clones of relative size $w_k$
with $\sum_k w_k = 1$. Give clone $k$ a somatic offset $\delta_k$ from its lineage mean at some
site, with mean zero and variance $\sigma^2$. The compartment's bulk beta is the size-weighted
mean, so

$$
\mathrm{Var}\Big[\sum_k w_k \delta_k\Big] = \sigma^2 \sum_k w_k^2
   = \frac{\sigma^2}{N_{\text{eff}}},
\qquad N_{\text{eff}} = \Big(\sum_k w_k^2\Big)^{-1}
$$

and $\sum_k w_k^2$ is exactly the Simpson index. The variance a clonal compartment contributes to
bulk methylation is inversely proportional to its **effective number of clones**, and clone count
enters through that quantity and no other. Three equal clones carry one cell's somatic state at
full weight; ten thousand clones average it to nothing.

This is why the effect is invisible to composition adjustment: $f$ can be identical between two
donors while $N_{\text{eff}}$ differs thousand-fold, and every published blood clock sees only $f$.

The myeloid version of the question is settled. Nachun et al. [[71]](references.qmd#ref-71)
measured clonal hematopoiesis against six clocks and found 1.31 years of acceleration on GrimAge
to 3.08 on extrinsic EEAA. The lymphoid analogue has not been asked.

### Measuring it

```python
div = fa.repertoire_diversity(clones, sample_col="sample_id", count_col="count")
data.obs = data.obs.join(div)

res = fa.score(data, clocks="compatible")
acc = fa.acceleration(res, adjust=["clonality", "cd8mem_fraction"])
```

`fa.acceleration` already accepts arbitrary `obs` columns as covariates, so the incremental test
is one call. The question is entirely whether clonality adds variance beyond cell fraction.

Depth is the trap. Richness and Shannon both rise with sequencing depth, so an unrarefied
comparison between a deeply and a shallowly sequenced donor measures the library rather than the
donor. Pass `rarefy="min"` to subsample every donor to a common depth by multivariate
hypergeometric draw, which is what a shallower run would actually have produced; sampling with
replacement inflates richness at low depth, in the same direction as the bias being corrected.
`clonality`, `simpson` and `effective_clones` are far more stable and are the ones to trust when
rarefaction is not possible.

### Simulating it

The mechanism arm needs no paired cohort. `fa.simulate_clonality` generates bulk methylomes at
**fixed** cell fractions and varying clone structure, so anything a clock does in response is
clone structure alone.

```python
sim = fa.simulate_clonality(
    reference, {"CD8mem": 0.3, "Neu": 0.7},
    clonal_types=["CD8mem"],
    clone_sizes=[fa.immune.zipf_clone_sizes(n, alpha=1.0)
                 for n in (2, 20, 200, 2000)],
    n_replicates=20)
res = fa.score(sim, clocks="compatible")
```

`reference` is sorted-cell mean beta, features by cell type. It is **not bundled**: every
deconvolution model in the registry is catalogued as `untraced`, carrying real metadata but no
coefficients, so the reference has to be supplied. `FlowSorted.Blood.EPIC` on Bioconductor is the
usual source.

::: {.callout-note}
## What the simulation returns on the test corpus

Across 42 clocks scored on 48 simulated samples at identical cell fractions, the median log-log
slope of score spread against effective clone count is **-0.494**, interquartile range -0.559 to
-0.415. The derivation predicts -0.5 and was not fitted to the simulation.

Among the clocks reporting years, `dnamphenoage` moves **4.35 years** between an
effectively-two-clone compartment and a diverse one, and `horvath2013` moves 1.54 years. Both fall
below a year once the compartment holds a few hundred effective clones.

Cell-type fractions were identical for every one of those samples, so composition adjustment
cannot remove any of it.
:::

## Where a clock's weight sits

A clock is a weight vector over CpGs, and two questions about that vector need no samples at all.

**Is this clock exposed to genotype?** If a clock CpG is under strong meQTL control and the allele
frequency at that variant differs between ancestral populations, a systematic difference in clock
output between ancestry groups follows from genotype frequency alone, with no difference in aging.
Cruz-Gonzalez et al. [[75]](references.qmd#ref-75) established that the major clocks lose accuracy in
admixed individuals; whether the size of that loss tracks each clock's meQTL exposure is open, and
half of that measurement is a property of the coefficients.

**Is this clock regulatory?** Patel et al. [[76]](references.qmd#ref-76) report that most CpGs used
by established clocks do *not* overlap known transcription factor binding sites. Reproducing that
against any annotation class is the same computation with a different list.

```python
mass = fa.coefficient_mass({"meqtl": godmc_cpgs, "enhancer": enhancer_cpgs})
```

### Why mass and not count

Counting annotated sites answers the wrong question. A clock's behaviour is driven by its heavy
features: a 353-CpG clock with two enormous weights and 351 small ones behaves like a two-CpG
clock. The statistic is therefore the share of $\sum_j |w_j|$ on annotated sites, with the plain
count returned beside it. **When the two diverge, the annotated sites are the heavy ones, and that
divergence is the finding.**

Run on the registry with each clock's own CpG set as the annotation, which needs no external file,
`horvath2013` shares 11.6 per cent of its *sites* with `dnamphenoage` but 19.6 per cent of its
*mass*. `weidner` shares two of its three sites with `dnamphenoage` and 89 per cent of its mass.
Two clocks that share their heaviest features will agree with each other for reasons that have
nothing to do with either being right.

FALCONAge bundles no annotation list. meQTL catalogues and regulatory builds are large, versioned
and separately licensed, and freezing one into a wheel would make it silently stale. GoDMC and the
EPIGEN meQTL database are the usual sources for the first question, the Ensembl Regulatory Build
or a Roadmap chromatin-state track for the second. `.attrs["unmatched"]` reports how many supplied
ids matched nothing, which is the check that catches an EPIC v2 list with `_TC21` suffixes meeting
bare `cg` probe ids.

## Reliability: trait, state and technical

A published ICC answers "how reproducible is this clock across a cohort". Someone asking "has my
number moved" needs a different quantity, and the gap between the two is why clock ICCs in the
literature read as reassuring while replicate disagreement of up to nine years is also true
[[68]](references.qmd#ref-68).

`fa.variance_components` separates them, given repeated measurement:

$$
y_{ijk} = \mu + a_i + s_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ijk}
$$

for person $i$, occasion $j$, replicate $k$, fitted by Henderson's method of moments. Two ICCs come
back and the gap between them is the point:

`icc`
: On raw scores. Comparable to what the literature publishes.

`icc_age_adjusted`
: The same after chronological age is regressed out. A cohort spanning decades holds most of its
  between-person variance in the age term, so a raw ICC largely reports that the clock tracks age,
  which was never in question. The adjusted figure is between-person reliability among people of
  the same age, which is what any individual-level claim rests on.

A clock whose raw ICC is 0.98 and whose adjusted ICC is 0.4 is not a precise instrument. It is a
cohort with a wide age range.

```python
vc = fa.variance_components(res, subject_col="donor", occasion_col="visit")
vc.table                      # var_trait, var_state, var_tech, icc, icc_age_adjusted
vc.replicates_needed(0.9)     # per occasion, to reach ICC 0.9
```

`replicates_needed` returns `inf` where no number of replicates gets there, and that is the
informative case rather than an error. Replicates average away the *technical* term only, so a
clock whose day-to-day within-person variance already exceeds the budget cannot be rescued by
running the array again. The honest answer is then a second draw, not a second scan.

Components are not clipped at zero. A negative one means the within-level spread exceeded the
between-level spread, which is real for a small design or a clock measuring nothing in this cohort,
and rounding it to zero disguises both.

## Mosaic ages within a tissue

`fa.models.single_cell.scage` gives an age per cell [[28]](references.qmd#ref-28). A bulk clock already reports the
mean, so the quantity worth having is the *shape* of the distribution underneath it: a tissue whose
cells are uniformly middle-aged and one holding a mixture of young and very old cells have the same
bulk methylation and, plausibly, very different biology.

The obstacle is that single-cell methylation coverage is sparse, so each per-cell age rests on few
sites and carries large error. Observed spread is therefore always positive, and reporting it as
heterogeneity is the mistake `fa.mosaic` exists to avoid.

The null is stated plainly: **every cell in the group has the same true age, and all observed
spread is estimation error**. It is simulated by drawing each cell from a normal centred on the
group mean with that cell's own standard error, taken from the profile-likelihood width `scage`
already returns.

```python
ages = fa.models.single_cell.scage(cells, reference)
mos  = fa.mosaic(ages, group="tissue")
```

A small `p_excess` is evidence of genuine mosaicism. A large one says the data cannot distinguish a
mosaic tissue from a uniform one measured badly, which at typical single-cell coverage is the usual
answer and is worth reporting as such. `n_at_grid_edge` counts cells whose estimate landed on the
boundary of the age grid, where the likelihood was truncated rather than maximised; those pile up
and inflate the tails, so a group with many of them should have its skew and kurtosis ignored.

## What none of this is

None of these functions is a clock, and none returns an age. They carry no coefficients, no
`scale_type` gate applies, and their outputs move with normalisation, probe panel and detection-p
filtering. The only defensible comparison is within one processed matrix.

That is a real constraint rather than a disclaimer. Entropy computed on noob-normalised betas and
entropy computed on raw betas are different numbers for the same DNA, and neither is more correct
than the other.
